rows.description: A teenager delays a project because a poor result would reveal weakness; putting it off protects the self-image but makes the eventual work worse.

rows.subtype: Stage 1: Task feels big or dull [Actor]
rows.description: A child looks at a project or homework and feels a small wave of dread or boredom. The mind wants relief now, so it moves to something easier, such as a game or a snack.
A teenager delays a project because a poor result would reveal weakness; putting it off protects the self-image but makes the eventual work worse.

The person asks what exactly feels uncomfortable, whether it is fear of being judged, unclear steps or boredom. Naming the feeling separates it from the task and points to a fix such as clarifying or asking for help.
A teenager shrugs off a flood or cyclone warning because nothing bad has happened before, and keeps scrolling, feeling safe because the world so far has been ordinary.

rows.subtype: Approach: wait and see because it may not be serious [Pitfall]
rows.description: Having seen earlier warnings pass with little harm, the person stays put until water enters the ground floor. Normalcy bias delays leaving until the routes are cut.

rows.subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
rows.description: A child with an external locus says the teacher gave low marks and never links results with preparation; belief that outcomes come from outside reduces effort.
A wise teenager asks what is within their control today and takes one action on it. Pairing effort with acceptance of what cannot be changed keeps hope without self-blame.
A child who stumbles while reading makes a silly face and gets the class laughing with them; the joke keeps control of the moment, though constant clowning can hide worry.
A school-age child enjoys puns, riddles and wordplay based on double meanings. Such humour signals growing language awareness and a wish to share fun and be part of the group.

rows.subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
rows.description: A child declares boredom after ten minutes and wants a screen; boredom is uncomfortable but can also be the doorway to imagination when adults give time and simple materials.
A schoolchild reads an adult's sigh or huff as tiredness, boredom or annoyance. It is ambiguous and may be relief; asking is everything is fine can prevent a child from assuming they are the cause.
